analysis.one_liner: Sunsets the federal tax code unless Congress approves a replacement, and creates a commission to propose one.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 9 Senate Republicans, never received a committee vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set an expiration date on the entire federal income tax code after 2014, keeping only Social Security and payroll taxes in place. It would have created a 19-member commission to study whether to replace the income tax with a flat tax, a national sales tax, or a simpler income tax. Congress would have had to approve a new tax system by July 2013, or vote to keep the current code. The bill never moved past its committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the immediate beneficiaries would have been small businesses and households that bear heavy paperwork costs under the current code, since the bill commits Congress to a simpler system. Beyond that, who gains depends entirely on what replacement Congress approves: the alternatives the bill directs the commission to study, a flat tax and a national sales tax, would tend to lower taxes on high earners and corporations and shift more of the burden onto households that spend most of their income.

how_it_helps.text: Terminates the Internal Revenue Code for taxable years beginning after 2013, except Social Security, self-employment, and railroad retirement payroll taxes.
Creates a National Commission on Tax Reform and Simplification with 19 members, at least 4 drawn from businesses with fewer than 50 employees, to recommend fundamental reform within 18 months.
Forces a congressional decision: a new federal tax system must be approved by July 4, 2013, or Congress must vote to reauthorize the existing code, putting an expiration date on the status quo.

analysis.who_pays: Depends on the replacement Congress approves. A national sales tax or flat tax would generally fall harder on middle- and lower-income households, who spend most of their income, and easier on high earners and corporations. Even before a replacement, the hard deadline creates risk: if Congress could not agree by 2013, the country could face a rushed choice or a tax system that lapses entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-income households under sales/flat tax options

drawbacks.text: The bill sunsets the entire income tax code without naming a replacement, leaving families and businesses unable to plan and creating the risk of a rushed or gridlocked decision by the July 2013 deadline.

The replacement options the bill instructs the commission to study, a flat tax and a national sales tax, would generally reduce progressivity: a national sales tax takes a larger share of income from households that spend most of what they earn, and a flat tax removes the higher rates on top earners.

The bill does not itself simplify anything; it creates a commission whose recommendations Congress could ignore, while the procedural deadline alone injects years of uncertainty into tax planning for households and businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea has a real appeal: the tax code is genuinely complex and compliance costs fall on everyone, especially small businesses. But this bill is a forcing device, not a reform. It sunsets the existing code without specifying what replaces it, and the alternatives it names would likely shift the tax burden away from high earners and onto ordinary wage earners. A deadline without a plan risks either a regressive rushed choice or a disruptive standoff.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Johnny Isakson introduced the Tax Code Termination Act on February 25, 2010, joined by original cosponsors Chambliss, Graham, Brownback, Hutchison, and Crapo.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
Eight senators cosponsored the bill, all Republicans.
The bill received no further action, no hearing, markup, or vote, and expired at the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax code stayed in place untouched, along with everyone who benefits from it as written, including the tax preparation industry built on its complexity and filers who benefit from current deductions and rates. No one's taxes changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax code and its beneficiaries

for.name: Sen. Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: 8 of 40 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Chambliss, Graham, Brownback, Hutchison, and Crapo
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican from outside the party supported it on the record.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it received no action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee never took the bill up; no vote was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software companies
industries.note: A wholesale replacement or drastic simplification of the tax code would shrink the market for paid filing help, which exists largely because the code is complex. Ordinary filers' compliance costs are the revenue base for this industry, so their interest runs against simplification.

Small firms face heavy filing and compliance costs under the current code, which the bill directs the commission to examine and would commit Congress to reducing. But whatever new tax system replaced the code could raise their taxes in other ways, so the net effect depends on the eventual replacement.

The bill itself changes no rates, but the alternatives it directs the commission to study, a flat tax and a national sales tax, would generally cut taxes substantially for top earners and profitable corporations while shifting more of the load onto consumption, which weighs heaviest on ordinary households.
